stem: Money is best defined as __________.
options: Anything that is generally accepted as a medium of exchange and a means of payment
solution: MONEY is anything that is GENERALLY ACCEPTED as a MEDIUM of EXCHANGE and a MEANS of PAYMENT for goods, services, and debts. Its essential feature is general acceptability. It includes currency (coins and notes) and demand deposits in banks, not only gold or paper. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Before money, exchange took place through the barter system, whose main drawback was __________.
options: The lack of double coincidence of wants
solution: The BARTER SYSTEM (direct exchange of goods for goods) suffered mainly from the LACK of a DOUBLE COINCIDENCE of WANTS — for exchange to occur, each party had to want exactly what the other offered, which was often impossible. Money solved this by acting as a common medium of exchange. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The function of money as a 'medium of exchange' means that __________.
options: Money is used to buy and sell goods and services, removing the need for double coincidence of wants
Money measures the value of goods
Money is used to repay debts only
solution: As a MEDIUM of EXCHANGE, MONEY is USED to BUY and SELL goods and services — people sell goods for money and use that money to buy other goods. This REMOVES the need for a DOUBLE COINCIDENCE of WANTS, greatly facilitating trade. It is the primary function of money. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The function of money as a 'unit of account' (measure of value) means that __________.
options: The values of all goods and services are expressed and compared in terms of money
Money is stored for the future
solution: As a UNIT of ACCOUNT (MEASURE of VALUE), money provides a COMMON MEASURE in which the VALUES of ALL goods and services are EXPRESSED and COMPARED (as prices). This makes accounting, comparison, and calculation of value possible. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The function of money as a 'store of value' means that __________.
options: Money can be held/saved to transfer purchasing power to the future
Money is only a medium of exchange
solution: As a STORE of VALUE, MONEY can be HELD or SAVED to TRANSFER PURCHASING POWER to the FUTURE — because it is durable and generally accepted, people can store wealth in the form of money and use it later. (Inflation, however, erodes this function.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The function of money as a 'standard of deferred payments' means that __________.
options: Money is used to make future/deferred payments and settle debts over time
Money has no role in credit
Money is only for current purchases
solution: As a STANDARD of DEFERRED PAYMENTS, MONEY is used to make FUTURE (DEFERRED) PAYMENTS and to SETTLE DEBTS over time — borrowing and lending are expressed in money terms, and loans are repaid in money. This function underlies the entire credit system. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Fiat money' is money that __________.
options: Is declared legal tender by government order and is accepted though it has no intrinsic value
solution: FIAT MONEY is money DECLARED to be LEGAL TENDER by GOVERNMENT ORDER (fiat) and accepted in payment even though it has NO INTRINSIC VALUE (it is not backed by gold or a commodity). Modern currency notes and coins are fiat money — accepted because the law and public confidence support them. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Legal tender' money is money that __________.
options: Must legally be accepted in settlement of debts and payments; refusal is not permitted
solution: LEGAL TENDER money is money that, by LAW, MUST be ACCEPTED in the SETTLEMENT of DEBTS and payments — a creditor cannot legally refuse it. In India, currency notes and coins are legal tender. (Cheques and other instruments are not legal tender, as their acceptance is optional.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The money supply of a country consists mainly of __________.
options: Currency (notes and coins) held by the public plus demand deposits in banks
solution: The MONEY SUPPLY (stock of money held by the public) consists mainly of CURRENCY (notes and COINS) HELD by the PUBLIC PLUS DEMAND DEPOSITS (chequable deposits) in BANKS. (Broader measures also include time deposits and post office savings.) It excludes money held by the government and banks themselves. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In the money supply measures, M1 (narrow money) consists of __________.
options: Currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with the RBI
solution: M1 (NARROW MONEY) = CURRENCY (notes and coins) with the PUBLIC + DEMAND DEPOSITS with the banking system + OTHER DEPOSITS with the RBI. It captures the most liquid forms of money used directly for transactions. Broader measures (M2, M3, M4) add successively less liquid deposits. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The central bank of India is the __________.
solution: The CENTRAL BANK of India is the RESERVE BANK of INDIA (RBI), established in 1935. It is the apex monetary authority that issues currency, controls the money supply and credit, acts as banker to the government and to banks, and regulates the banking system. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The sole authority to issue currency notes (except one-rupee notes/coins) in India rests with the __________.
solution: The RESERVE BANK of INDIA has the SOLE AUTHORITY (monopoly) to ISSUE CURRENCY NOTES in India (the one-rupee note and coins are issued by the Government of India, though circulated by the RBI). Being the sole issuer gives the RBI control over the currency component of the money supply. So option 1 is correct.

stem: As the 'banker to the government', the RBI __________.
options: Keeps the government's accounts, manages its receipts and payments, and manages public debt
Collects income tax directly from individuals
solution: As the BANKER to the GOVERNMENT, the RBI KEEPS the GOVERNMENT's ACCOUNTS, MANAGES its RECEIPTS and PAYMENTS, provides short-term loans (ways and means advances), and MANAGES the PUBLIC DEBT (issuing and servicing government securities). It handles the government's banking business. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The RBI is called the 'lender of last resort' because it __________.
options: Provides loans/credit to commercial banks in times of financial difficulty when they cannot borrow elsewhere
solution: The RBI is the LENDER of LAST RESORT because it PROVIDES LOANS/CREDIT to COMMERCIAL BANKS in TIMES of FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY (liquidity crises) when they cannot borrow from other sources. This support maintains confidence and stability in the banking system and prevents bank failures from spreading. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Commercial banks perform the crucial function of accepting deposits and __________.
options: Advancing loans (lending) to businesses and individuals
solution: COMMERCIAL BANKS perform two crucial functions: ACCEPTING DEPOSITS from the public (savings, current, and fixed deposits) and ADVANCING LOANS (LENDING) to businesses and individuals. By channelling savings into loans, they mobilise funds and, through credit creation, expand the money supply. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Commercial banks are able to 'create money' (credit) because __________.
options: They keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest, which returns as new deposits, expanding total deposits
They receive gifts from the RBI
solution: Commercial banks CREATE MONEY (credit) through the FRACTIONAL RESERVE system: they keep only a FRACTION of DEPOSITS as RESERVES and LEND OUT the REST. The loaned money is spent and RETURNS to the banking system as NEW DEPOSITS, which are again partly lent out — so total deposits (and the money supply) EXPAND to a MULTIPLE of the initial deposit. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'money multiplier' is __________.
options: The ratio by which total deposits/money supply expand from a given change in reserves (roughly 1 divided by the reserve ratio)
The number of banks in a country
solution: The MONEY MULTIPLIER is the RATIO by which TOTAL DEPOSITS (and money supply) EXPAND from a given change in bank RESERVES (high-powered money). In the simplest case it equals 1 ÷ the RESERVE RATIO — the lower the reserve ratio, the larger the multiplier and the greater the credit creation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'Cash Reserve Ratio' (CRR) is __________.
options: The fraction of banks' total deposits that they must keep as cash reserves with the RBI
solution: The CASH RESERVE RATIO (CRR) is the FRACTION (percentage) of banks' TOTAL DEPOSITS (net demand and time liabilities) that they must keep as CASH RESERVES with the RBI. Raising the CRR reduces the funds banks can lend (contracting credit); lowering it increases lending capacity. It is a key instrument of monetary control. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'Statutory Liquidity Ratio' (SLR) requires banks to __________.
options: Maintain a minimum fraction of their deposits in the form of liquid assets like cash, gold, and approved government securities
solution: The STATUTORY LIQUIDITY RATIO (SLR) requires banks to MAINTAIN a MINIMUM FRACTION of their DEPOSITS in the form of LIQUID ASSETS — such as CASH, GOLD, and approved GOVERNMENT SECURITIES — with themselves (in addition to CRR held with the RBI). Changing the SLR affects banks' capacity to create credit. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'repo rate' is the rate at which __________.
options: The RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks (against government securities)
Banks lend to their best customers
Foreign banks lend to the RBI
solution: The REPO RATE (repurchase rate) is the rate at which the RBI LENDS SHORT-TERM funds to COMMERCIAL BANKS, against the collateral of GOVERNMENT SECURITIES. A HIGHER repo rate makes borrowing from the RBI costlier, tending to reduce credit and money supply; a LOWER repo rate encourages borrowing and lending. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'reverse repo rate' is the rate at which __________.
options: The RBI borrows from commercial banks (banks park their surplus funds with the RBI)
solution: The REVERSE REPO RATE is the rate at which the RBI BORROWS from COMMERCIAL BANKS — i.e., banks PARK their SURPLUS FUNDS with the RBI and earn this rate. Raising the reverse repo rate encourages banks to keep money with the RBI (reducing money in circulation); it is used to absorb excess liquidity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'bank rate' is __________.
options: The rate at which the RBI provides long-term loans/rediscounts bills to commercial banks
The rate banks pay on savings deposits
solution: The BANK RATE is the rate at which the RBI provides LONG-TERM LOANS to (or REDISCOUNTS the bills of) COMMERCIAL BANKS. Like the repo rate, RAISING the bank rate raises the cost of borrowing from the RBI, discouraging credit expansion; LOWERING it encourages credit. It is a traditional instrument of monetary policy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Open Market Operations' (OMO) by the RBI refer to __________.
options: The buying and selling of government securities in the open market to control the money supply
The opening of new bank branches
solution: OPEN MARKET OPERATIONS (OMO) refer to the RBI's BUYING and SELLING of GOVERNMENT SECURITIES in the OPEN MARKET to control the MONEY SUPPLY. SELLING securities absorbs money from the system (reducing money supply); BUYING securities injects money (increasing money supply). It is a flexible quantitative tool of monetary policy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The instruments of monetary policy are broadly divided into quantitative (general) and __________ instruments.
solution: The instruments of MONETARY POLICY are broadly divided into QUANTITATIVE (GENERAL) instruments — which affect the overall volume of credit (CRR, SLR, repo rate, bank rate, OMO) — and QUALITATIVE (SELECTIVE) instruments — which affect the direction/allocation of credit to particular sectors (margin requirements, moral suasion, credit rationing, etc.). So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Margin requirement' is a qualitative credit control tool that refers to __________.
options: The difference between the value of the security/collateral and the amount of loan granted against it
The interest rate on all loans
The reserve kept with the RBI
solution: The MARGIN REQUIREMENT is the DIFFERENCE between the VALUE of the SECURITY (COLLATERAL) pledged and the AMOUNT of LOAN granted against it. RAISING the margin means borrowers can get smaller loans against the same security (contracting credit to that sector); LOWERING it expands credit. It is a SELECTIVE (qualitative) tool. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Moral suasion' as a monetary policy tool means __________.
options: The RBI persuading and advising banks (through requests and meetings) to follow desired credit policies
solution: MORAL SUASION is a QUALITATIVE tool where the RBI PERSUADES and ADVISES banks — through REQUESTS, letters, and MEETINGS — to follow DESIRED CREDIT POLICIES (e.g., to restrain or expand lending). It relies on persuasion and cooperation rather than legal compulsion. So option 1 is correct.

stem: To control INFLATION (too much money/demand), the RBI would generally adopt a __________ monetary policy.
options: Contractionary (tight) policy — raising CRR, SLR, repo rate and selling securities to reduce money supply
solution: To control INFLATION (excess money and demand), the RBI adopts a CONTRACTIONARY (TIGHT) MONETARY POLICY: RAISING the CRR, SLR, REPO RATE, and bank rate, and SELLING government securities (OMO). These measures REDUCE the MONEY SUPPLY and credit, dampening aggregate demand and price rises. So option 1 is correct.

stem: To combat a recession/deflation (deficient demand), the RBI would adopt an __________ monetary policy.
options: Expansionary (easy) policy — lowering CRR, SLR and repo rate and buying securities to increase money supply
solution: To combat a RECESSION/DEFLATION (deficient demand), the RBI adopts an EXPANSIONARY (EASY/cheap money) MONETARY POLICY: LOWERING the CRR, SLR, REPO RATE, and bank rate, and BUYING government securities (OMO). These INCREASE the MONEY SUPPLY and credit, encouraging borrowing, investment, and spending to revive demand. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'High-powered money' (or reserve money / monetary base) consists of __________.
options: Currency held by the public plus reserves of commercial banks (which is issued by the RBI)
solution: HIGH-POWERED MONEY (RESERVE MONEY, monetary base) consists of CURRENCY (notes and coins) HELD by the PUBLIC PLUS the RESERVES of COMMERCIAL BANKS (their cash and deposits with the RBI). It is created by the RBI, and through the money multiplier it supports a larger total money supply. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Demand deposits are considered part of money supply because __________.
options: They can be withdrawn on demand and transferred by cheque, so they are used to make payments like currency
They are the same as gold
solution: DEMAND DEPOSITS (like current and savings account balances) are part of the MONEY SUPPLY because they can be WITHDRAWN on DEMAND and TRANSFERRED by CHEQUE (or now digitally), so people USE them to MAKE PAYMENTS just like currency. Their high liquidity makes them money in the transactions sense. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A cheque is NOT money (not legal tender) but is __________.
options: A negotiable instrument/order to a bank to pay a sum from the drawer's account; its acceptance is voluntary
Legal tender that must be accepted
Printed by the RBI as currency
solution: A CHEQUE is NOT money (not LEGAL TENDER) but a NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENT — an ORDER to a BANK to PAY a specified sum from the DRAWER's ACCOUNT to the payee. Its ACCEPTANCE is VOLUNTARY (a person may refuse a cheque), unlike currency notes which must be accepted. It is a convenient means of transferring demand deposits. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): An increase in the CRR reduces the money supply. Reason (R): A higher CRR forces banks to keep more of their deposits as reserves, leaving less to lend and create credit. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: A is TRUE — an INCREASE in the CRR REDUCES the money supply. R is TRUE and correctly EXPLAINS A: a HIGHER CRR FORCES banks to keep MORE of their deposits as RESERVES with the RBI, leaving LESS available to LEND and CREATE CREDIT — which reduces the money multiplier and the money supply. So R is the correct explanation of A. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The primary goals of monetary policy typically include __________.
options: Price stability (controlling inflation) and supporting economic growth and financial stability
solution: The PRIMARY GOALS of MONETARY POLICY typically include PRICE STABILITY (controlling INFLATION) while also supporting ECONOMIC GROWTH, EMPLOYMENT, and FINANCIAL STABILITY. In India, the RBI conducts monetary policy with a primary objective of maintaining price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth. So option 1 is correct.

stem: If the RBI wants to increase liquidity in the banking system, it can __________.
options: Buy government securities in the open market and/or reduce the CRR
Sell government securities and raise the CRR
solution: To INCREASE LIQUIDITY (money) in the banking system, the RBI can BUY GOVERNMENT SECURITIES in the open market (injecting cash) and/or REDUCE the CRR (freeing up bank reserves for lending). Selling securities, raising the CRR/SLR, or raising the repo rate would instead reduce liquidity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The value of money is inversely related to the price level, meaning that when prices rise (inflation), __________.
options: The purchasing power (value) of money falls
Prices and money value both rise together
solution: The VALUE of MONEY (its PURCHASING POWER) is INVERSELY related to the PRICE LEVEL. When PRICES RISE (INFLATION), each unit of money buys FEWER goods, so the PURCHASING POWER (value) of money FALLS. Conversely, when prices fall, the value of money rises. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches a tool with its effect when its value is RAISED by the RBI?
options: Raise CRR → less money supply; Raise repo rate → costlier borrowing, less credit; Sell securities (OMO) → absorb money
Raise CRR → more lending; Raise repo rate → cheaper loans; Sell securities → inject money
All tools increase the money supply when raised
solution: When RAISED by the RBI: a higher CRR means banks hold MORE reserves, so LESS MONEY SUPPLY/credit; a higher REPO RATE makes borrowing from the RBI COSTLIER, reducing credit; SELLING securities (OMO) ABSORBS MONEY from the system. All these are CONTRACTIONARY. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'demand for money' arises mainly from two motives: the transaction motive and the __________ motive.
solution: The DEMAND for MONEY (why people wish to hold money) arises mainly from the TRANSACTION MOTIVE (holding money to carry out day-to-day PURCHASES) and the SPECULATIVE MOTIVE (holding money to take advantage of expected changes in bond prices/interest rates). Keynes also noted a precautionary motive. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The transaction demand for money is directly related to __________.
options: The level of income/transactions (higher income → more money held for transactions)
solution: The TRANSACTION DEMAND for money is DIRECTLY (positively) related to the LEVEL of INCOME and the volume of TRANSACTIONS — the HIGHER the income and the more goods people buy, the MORE MONEY they need to HOLD to carry out their day-to-day transactions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The speculative demand for money is inversely related to __________.
options: The rate of interest (higher interest → less money held, as bonds become more attractive)
solution: The SPECULATIVE DEMAND for money is INVERSELY related to the RATE of INTEREST. When interest rates are HIGH, holding money has a high opportunity cost (bonds pay more and their prices are low/expected to rise), so people hold LESS money and more bonds; when interest is LOW, they hold MORE money. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a NON-legal-tender (optional) money?
options: A cheque or a bank draft
solution: A CHEQUE or a bank DRAFT is NON-LEGAL-TENDER (OPTIONAL) money — its acceptance is voluntary and a person can refuse it. CURRENCY NOTES and COINS are LEGAL TENDER, which must be accepted in payment. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In India, the currency notes issued by the RBI are backed by the __________ system of note issue.
options: Minimum reserve system (a minimum reserve of gold and foreign securities is maintained)
Full gold backing for every note
solution: In India, currency notes are issued under the MINIMUM RESERVE SYSTEM: the RBI keeps a MINIMUM RESERVE of GOLD and FOREIGN SECURITIES (a fixed statutory minimum) and can issue currency beyond this based on the needs of the economy. This gives flexibility, unlike a full-backing system where every note must be backed by gold. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'bankers' bank' function of the RBI means that it __________.
options: Holds the reserves of commercial banks, provides them loans, and acts as a clearing house for interbank transactions
solution: As the BANKERS' BANK, the RBI HOLDS the CASH RESERVES of COMMERCIAL BANKS (CRR deposits), PROVIDES them with LOANS/rediscount facilities (lender of last resort), and acts as a CLEARING HOUSE for settling INTERBANK TRANSACTIONS. It stands in the same relation to commercial banks as they do to their customers. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A fall in the reserve ratio (CRR/SLR) will, other things equal, cause the money multiplier to __________.
solution: Since the money multiplier is inversely related to the reserve ratio (roughly 1 ÷ reserve ratio), a FALL in the RESERVE RATIO (CRR/SLR) will cause the MONEY MULTIPLIER to INCREASE — banks can lend a larger share of deposits, so a given amount of reserves supports MORE credit creation and a larger money supply. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Time deposits' (fixed deposits) differ from demand deposits in that time deposits __________.
options: Are payable only after a fixed period and are not withdrawable on demand by cheque, so they are less liquid
Can be withdrawn anytime by cheque
solution: TIME DEPOSITS (FIXED DEPOSITS) are payable only after a FIXED PERIOD (maturity) and are NOT withdrawable on demand by cheque, making them LESS LIQUID than demand deposits — but they earn higher interest. Because they are less liquid, they are part of broader money measures (M3) rather than narrow money (M1). So option 1 is correct.

stem: The primary distinction between M1 and M3 (broad money) is that M3 additionally includes __________.
options: Net time deposits of the public with the banking system
solution: The main distinction is that M3 (BROAD MONEY) = M1 + NET TIME DEPOSITS of the public with the banking system. M1 (narrow money) includes only the most liquid components (currency, demand deposits, other deposits with RBI), while M3 adds the less-liquid TIME (fixed) DEPOSITS. M3 is the most commonly watched money-supply aggregate. So option 1 is correct.

stem: If the RBI raises the repo rate, commercial banks are likely to __________.
options: Raise their own lending rates, making loans costlier and tending to reduce borrowing and spending
solution: If the RBI RAISES the REPO RATE (the rate at which banks borrow from the RBI), banks' cost of funds rises, so they tend to RAISE their OWN LENDING RATES. This makes LOANS COSTLIER, tending to REDUCE BORROWING, investment, and spending — a contractionary effect used to curb inflation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Credit rationing' as a selective credit control means the RBI __________.
options: Fixes limits on the amount of credit available for particular purposes or sectors
solution: CREDIT RATIONING is a SELECTIVE (qualitative) credit control in which the RBI FIXES LIMITS on the AMOUNT of CREDIT available for PARTICULAR PURPOSES or SECTORS — restricting credit to less-desirable/speculative uses while channelling it to priority sectors. It controls the direction, not just the total volume, of credit. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A key reason the general acceptability of money depends on trust/confidence is that __________.
options: Modern fiat money has no intrinsic value, so it works only because people are confident others will accept it too
solution: The general acceptability of modern FIAT MONEY depends on TRUST/CONFIDENCE because it has NO INTRINSIC VALUE (a paper note is just paper). It functions as money ONLY because people are CONFIDENT that OTHERS will ACCEPT it too (and because it is legal tender backed by the state). If confidence collapses, money can lose its acceptability. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following best summarises the difference between money and near-money?
options: Money is a means of payment directly usable in transactions; near-money (like time deposits, bonds) is a highly liquid asset that must first be converted into money
Near-money is legal tender but money is not
Near-money cannot be converted into money
solution: MONEY is a MEANS of PAYMENT DIRECTLY USABLE in transactions (currency, demand deposits). NEAR-MONEY refers to HIGHLY LIQUID ASSETS — such as TIME DEPOSITS, treasury bills, and BONDS — that are close substitutes for money but must FIRST be CONVERTED into money before being used to make payments. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Money and Banking' is that:
options: MONEY — anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange — overcame the barter problem of double coincidence of wants and performs four functions (medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payments); modern money is largely FIAT and LEGAL TENDER, and the MONEY SUPPLY consists of currency with the public plus bank deposits (M1, M2, M3, M4); COMMERCIAL BANKS accept deposits and lend, CREATING credit through the money multiplier; and the CENTRAL BANK (RBI) issues currency, acts as banker to the government and banker's bank and lender of last resort, and controls money and credit through quantitative tools (CRR, SLR, repo/reverse repo, bank rate, open market operations) and qualitative tools to achieve price stability and growth
solution: The chapter's overall message is that MONEY — ANYTHING GENERALLY ACCEPTED as a MEDIUM of EXCHANGE — solved the BARTER problem of the DOUBLE COINCIDENCE of WANTS and performs FOUR FUNCTIONS: MEDIUM of EXCHANGE, UNIT of ACCOUNT (measure of value), STORE of VALUE, and STANDARD of DEFERRED PAYMENTS. Modern money is largely FIAT MONEY and LEGAL TENDER, and the MONEY SUPPLY consists of CURRENCY held by the PUBLIC PLUS BANK DEPOSITS (measured as M1, M2, M3, M4). COMMERCIAL BANKS accept DEPOSITS and ADVANCE LOANS, CREATING CREDIT/money through the fractional-reserve MONEY MULTIPLIER. The CENTRAL BANK — the RESERVE BANK of INDIA — ISSUES CURRENCY, acts as BANKER to the GOVERNMENT, BANKERS' BANK, and LENDER of LAST RESORT, and CONTROLS money and credit using QUANTITATIVE tools (CRR, SLR, REPO/REVERSE REPO RATE, BANK RATE, OPEN MARKET OPERATIONS) and QUALITATIVE tools (margin requirements, moral suasion) to pursue PRICE STABILITY and GROWTH. So the overall message is option 2.
